title: Why Molasses Flooded Boston
topic: Why a wave of molasses flooded Boston streets in 1919

lines: A steel tank burst and a wall of syrup swallowed a Boston street.
People in the North End heard a roar like an elevated train.
It was January 15, 1919.
That tank held 2.3 million gallons of molasses.
It stood 50 feet tall and 90 feet wide.
The tank collapsed at about 12:30 in the afternoon.
Rivets shot out like machine gun fire.
A wave of molasses 25 feet high raced through the streets.
It moved at 35 miles per hour.
It swept buildings off their foundations.
It tipped a streetcar off its tracks.
It picked up a truck and threw it into the harbor.
The molasses killed 21 people and injured 150.
You see, molasses is 40% denser than water.
It's like trying to swim through warm honey that gets thicker as you struggle.
The real reason: the day before, a ship delivered warm molasses.
That warm molasses thinned the older, colder molasses already inside.
The tank couldn't hold the pressure.
When it burst, the molasses flowed fast, then cooled and thickened.
That sticky goo trapped people before rescuers could pull them free.
For decades after, Bostonians swore the North End still smelled of molasses on hot summer days.
The tank was never rebuilt.

claims.claim: The disaster occurred on January 15, 1919, in the North End neighborhood of Boston.
The tank contained 2.3 million US gallons of molasses, stood 50 feet tall and 90 feet in diameter.
The tank burst at approximately 12:30 p.m.
Witnesses reported hearing a roar similar to an elevated train and rivets shooting out like machine gun fire.
A wave of molasses 25 feet high at its peak moved at 35 mph.
The wave swept buildings off their foundations, tipped a streetcar off its tracks, and threw a truck into the harbor.
The disaster killed 21 people and injured 150.
Molasses is about 40% denser than water.
On the previous day, a ship had delivered a fresh load of molasses, which had been warmed to decrease its viscosity for transfer.
When the tank collapsed, the fluid cooled quickly as it spread, and the viscosity increased dramatically, hampering efforts to free victims before they suffocated.
Residents reported for decades afterwards that the area still smelled of molasses on hot summer days.
USIA did not rebuild the tank.
